title: Before you pick anything
points: Be 100% sure of what it is before you eat it — 99% is not enough. If in doubt, leave it out.
Check every feature, not just the picture. If one feature does not match, it is not that species.
Never eat a mushroom on the word of a photo, a website or an app alone.
Dig out the whole stem base instead of cutting the stem: a deadly Amanita's bag (volva) is often hidden in the soil or the leaves.
Leave small 'button' mushrooms: young ones do not show all their features, and young deadly Amanitas look like button mushrooms.
Keep anything you are not sure of away from mushrooms for eating, each kind in its own paper bag.

title: How to take a spore print
points: Cut off the stem and lay the cap gills-down on paper that is half white and half black, so any colour shows.
Cover it with a glass or a jar so it does not dry out.
Leave it for a few hours, or overnight, then lift the cap gently.
The colour points to the family: Amanitas print white, webcaps rust-brown, and Agaricus mushrooms (field and horse mushrooms) chocolate to purple-brown.
A white print from what you hoped was a field or horse mushroom is a warning: the deadly Amanitas print white.
A spore print alone cannot name a mushroom — it is one feature among many.

title: The deadly families to know in the UK
points: Amanitas — the Deathcap and the Destroying Angel: white gills, a ring, and a bag (volva) at the stem base. They cause most deaths from mushroom poisoning.
Small dapperlings (Lepiota): several carry the Deathcap's poison, and they are very hard to tell apart — eat none.
Webcaps (Cortinarius): the Deadly Webcap and the Fool's Webcap destroy the kidneys.
Fibrecaps (Inocybe): the Deadly Fibrecap has killed people.
Small white funnels (Clitocybe), such as the Fool's Funnel: they grow in lawns and fairy rings, where people pick the Fairy Ring Champignon.
The Funeral Bell: a small brown mushroom on dead wood, with the Deathcap's poison. It is mistaken for the Velvet Shank and the Sheathed Woodtuft.
Conecaps (Conocybe): small brown mushrooms with a ring, in gardens, leaf litter and woodchip, with the Deathcap's poison.

title: The rules in the UK
points: Ask the landowner first: taking fungi from land without the owner's permission can be against the law.
Some fungi are protected by law (Schedule 8 of the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981) and must not be picked at all — the Bearded Tooth (Lion's Mane) is one.
Check for local byelaws and codes: some places, such as the New Forest, have their own rules on picking fungi.
Take only a little, for your own use — never more than half of what you find — and leave the rest for wildlife.
Pick only opened caps, which have already shed their spores.

title: If someone has eaten a mushroom you are not sure of
points: Get medical help at once, even if they feel well — early treatment saves lives. Wild Food UK advises calling NHS 111 and taking any leftover mushroom, or photos of it.
The deadliest poisons give no early warning: the Deathcap's causes no symptoms for 6–12 hours, the webcaps' for days, sometimes two weeks.
After a Deathcap, the first sickness can pass for a day or two before the liver and kidneys fail — feeling better does not mean it is over.
